A Universal Asynchronous Receiver/Transmitter sends bytes with no shared clock line — timing is agreed in advance (the baud rate) and each byte is framed with start/stop bits so the receiver can find the edges on its own.

## Framing

Idle line sits high. A frame is: one start bit (line pulled low), 5–9 data bits (LSB first), an optional parity bit, then one or more stop bits (line released high):

$$
\text{frame bits} = 1 + \text{data bits} + [\text{parity?} 1 : 0] + \text{stop bits}
$$

Both ends must agree on baud rate, data bits, parity, and stop bits beforehand — there's no negotiation. Get any of the four wrong and you get garbage or nothing.

## Calculator: bit time and frame time

```{=html}
<div id="uart-calc"></div>
<script src="../assets/js/calc-engine.js"></script>
<script>
Calc.create({
  root: "uart-calc",
  inputs: [
    { id: "baud", label: "Baud rate", value: 115200, min: 1, step: 100 },
    { id: "dataBits", label: "Data bits", value: 8, min: 5, step: 1 },
    { id: "parity", label: "Parity", type: "select", value: "none", options: [
      { value: "none", label: "None" },
      { value: "even", label: "Even" },
      { value: "odd", label: "Odd" }
    ] },
    { id: "stopBits", label: "Stop bits", type: "select", value: "1", options: ["1", "1.5", "2"] }
  ],
  outputs: [
    { id: "bitTime", label: "Bit time" },
    { id: "frameBits", label: "Frame bits" },
    { id: "frameTime", label: "Frame time" }
  ],
  compute: function (v) {
    if (v.baud <= 0) return { bitTime: "-", frameBits: "-", frameTime: "-" };
    var bitTimeUs = 1e6 / v.baud;
    var parityBit = v.parity === "none" ? 0 : 1;
    var frameBits = 1 + v.dataBits + parityBit + parseFloat(v.stopBits);
    var frameTimeUs = frameBits * bitTimeUs;
    return {
      bitTime: bitTimeUs.toFixed(2) + " µs",
      frameBits: frameBits.toString(),
      frameTime: frameTimeUs.toFixed(2) + " µs"
    };
  }
});
</script>
```

## Implementing it in circuit

**Voltage levels first.** A microcontroller's UART pins swing between 0 V and its logic supply (3.3 V or 5 V) — that's TTL/CMOS-level UART, not RS-232 (see the next page). Connecting a 5 V UART TX directly into a 3.3 V-only RX pin can overstress the input; check the receiving device's absolute maximum, and add a level shifter or a simple resistor divider if there's any doubt.

**TX goes to RX.** Obvious once stated, a common wiring mistake otherwise — device A's TX connects to device B's RX, and vice versa. Boards labeled from the device's own perspective (a USB-serial adapter's "TX" is what *it* transmits) make this easy to get backwards.

**Common ground is mandatory.** UART is single-ended — the receiver decides high/low relative to its own ground pin. If the two devices don't share a ground reference (separate power supplies, long cable runs), add a ground wire alongside the signal wires, or use an isolated UART transceiver if the two sides genuinely need to float independently.

**Cable length and speed trade off.** Bare TTL-level UART over an unshielded wire is only reliable for short runs (tens of centimeters to maybe a meter, more at lower baud rates) before ringing and noise pickup cause errors — for anything longer, convert to RS-232 or RS-485 at the electrical layer instead of pushing raw TTL levels down a long cable.
